title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to test whether interposing a deterministic network verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated device configurations that would execute with operational faults in an isolated emulation environment. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical initial LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification) we evaluated 72 preregistered intent pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution and deterministic accounting show completed_episode_count = 144, model_calls_used = 72, and no technical failures. All 72 baseline executions produced no emulator‑observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected‑fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Confirmatory interpretation: for the chosen model, task bank, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, the verifier did not reduce undetected faults because none were observed in the baseline (a ceiling effect). We report preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, exact inferential outputs, and concrete limitations that motivate alternative designs (adversarial tasks, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model sampling) required to assess verifier utility under realistic error regimes.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate high‑level operator intent into low‑level device configurations, enabling new NetOps workflows but raising operational risk when generated configurations violate safety or policy invariants. Prior controlled studies demonstrate promising intent→configuration accuracy under constrained vendor dialects, while surveys and prototype systems emphasize semantic errors, command ordering mistakes, and protocol misuse that may cause outages or policy violations [1], [2]. A canonical mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that places deterministic validators (header‑space/ policy checkers) between generation and execution to detect violations before applying changes [3], [4]. However, direct preregistered empirical evidence quantifying how much a verifier reduces executed, undetected faults on realistic task banks is limited.

This work tests the preregistered research question (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001): Does coupling an LLM generator with a canonical deterministic network verifier materially reduce the proportion of LLM candidates that would execute with operational faults compared to executing the same candidate without verification when the identical candidate is evaluated under both conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics)? The paired shared_initial_candidate design isolates verifier detection performance on identical generator outputs, avoiding confounding from generator stochasticity.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired experiment with deterministic execution accounting and archived artifacts. (2) Exact, artifact‑grounded inferential outputs showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (zero baseline faults) and an evidence‑based discussion of design consequences. (3) Concrete recommendations and tractable alternative experimental contracts to measure verifier utility when generator error prevalence is nontrivial.
sections.related_work: LLM‑based intent→configuration translation has been empirically evaluated in constrained settings with measured task‑level accuracy; such studies underline promise but also caution about execution risk without verification [1]. Multi‑agent and tool‑augmented frameworks integrate validators and orchestration to reduce regressions in NetOps workflows; prototypes show integration patterns but generally lack standardized, preregistered end‑to‑end evaluation of verifier detection on execution outcomes [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures are proposed and instantiated in code repair and regulated engineering domains to combine stochastic generation with deterministic checks and repairs [3]; adaptation to network protocol semantics is plausible but underexplored in published empirical work. Classical network verification methods such as header‑space analysis provide efficient reachability and policy checks and are natural verifier candidates for NetOps GVR stacks [4]. Our study contributes an artifact‑grounded, preregistered empirical test that couples an LLM generator (gpt-5-mini) with a deterministic network verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and reports exact emulator outcomes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001; preregistration manifest SHA‑256 recorded in the evidence bundle) froze hypotheses, sampling, inclusion/exclusion rules, and the primary estimand before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Confirmatory hypothesis H1 prespecified a paired binary test designed to detect an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 (alpha = 0.05, power >= 0.80) and registered N = 72 paired intents stratified across three topology complexity strata.

Design semantics and shared_initial_candidate. The registered execution_contract specified generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate": for each intent a single initial LLM candidate was produced and that same candidate was evaluated in both baseline and guarded conditions. Baseline: execute the candidate in an isolated emulator and record emulator‑observed faults. Guarded: run the deterministic verifier on the same candidate; if the verifier flags a violation, the candidate is treated as prevented (not executed); otherwise the candidate is executed and the emulator outcome recorded. This design isolates verifier detection performance on identical generator outputs; it does not measure benefits that require alternative generations or repair-mediated improvements.

Model, adapter, and verifier. Initial generations declared requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The canonical verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version recorded as "5.0" in scoring traces). Validator scoring used the rule full_intent_constraint_validation and produced per‑episode structured traces (validation_before, validation_after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, violation_codes). The archived model_configuration.json shows temperature = null; this indicates provider default sampling semantics governed generation at runtime and is recorded as residual sampling‑parameter uncertainty in the artifacts.

Task bank, constraints, and contamination. Tasks were generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and include explicit intent, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, difficulty metadata, and expected_final_state. Exact‑match contamination checks against public corpora were preregistered; exact matches would be excluded from confirmatory analysis. In the executed run no confirmatory pairs were excluded; the contamination_summary.csv in analysis artifacts is empty.

Execution, retries, and missingness. The missingness_plan allowed up to two retries on transient hosted‑API errors. Execution manifest (execution_summary) records: planned_episode_count = 144, completed_episode_count = 144, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 72. Provider_call_audit aggregated hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, cache_miss_count = 72, and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 72. All retries and provider call outcomes are archived in deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution logs.

Scoring and analysis. Each episode received a binary score (valid configuration vs. violation) from deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and a detailed validator_trace. The primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute the paired contingency table and run an exact McNemar two‑sided test when applicable. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for descriptive rates used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 (recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). All analysis scripts and CSV artifacts are included in the archived evidence bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic consistency. The archived execution manifest confirms completion without technical failures: completed_episode_count = 144, model_calls_used = 72, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 72. Provider call audit fields show no cache hits and a single stage count of shared_initial_generation = 72. The analysis deterministic_reconciliation.json reports all deterministic consistency checks passed (all_deterministic_consistency_checks_passed = true) and pair accounting consistent.

Primary contingency and inferential outputs. The paired contingency table aggregated across 72 pairs is: n_11 = 72 (baseline succeeded and guarded succeeded), n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. The estimated paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) report baseline success_rate = 1.0 and guarded success_rate = 1.0. These numeric values are archived with SHA‑256 artifacts referenced in the evidence bundle.

Representative validator traces and scoring metadata. Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json) demonstrate validator internals for several tasks: parsed_command_count ranges from 2–6 for representative tasks; required_command_count equals parsed counts where the validator judged the candidate complete; difficulty.level values include "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" as labeled by the task generator. In these examples validator_version = "5.0" and score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION". The validator traces record normalized_configuration, validation_before and validation_after network states, and violation_count = 0 for the representative set; these artifacts confirm verifier operation on every shared candidate and the absence of flagged violations in this confirmatory sample.

Interpretation. The confirmatory outcome is degenerate: because the baseline executed identical candidates and produced no emulator‑observed faults, the verifier could not demonstrate a reduction in undetected faults. This ceiling effect is both a valid experimental observation under the preregistered estimand and a direct consequence of the shared_initial_candidate contract combined with a low baseline error prevalence on the chosen task bank and model configuration.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory interpretation and ceiling effect. The preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics validly measures verifier detection on identical outputs. Observing zero baseline faults yields a scientifically informative null/ceiling outcome: for the chosen prompts, dialects, and emulated tasks the generator outputs were uniformly valid on the emulator, and the verifier produced no additional prevention. This outcome should not be generalized to imply verifiers are unnecessary in other settings where generator errors are more frequent.

Design implications for future GVR evaluations. (1) Shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate detection but preclude measuring benefits that depend on repair or alternative generation; to evaluate repair‑mediated benefits the contract must permit repair calls and measure repaired outcomes. (2) Allowing independent per‑condition generation (separate model calls for baseline and guarded) or multi‑sample generations per task introduces generator variability and increases the probability of observing generator errors; such designs better test verifier detection and blocking efficacy across stochastic outputs. (3) Constructing adversarial/fault‑injection task sets (higher difficulty patterns, intentionally entangled dependencies) will produce non‑degenerate error regimes where verifier detection and false‑positive tradeoffs can be measured.

Threats to validity and operational caveats. Internal validity: the run used one shared generation per intent and the archived model_configuration.json shows temperature = null; runtime provider defaults governed stochasticity and thus sampling‑parameter provenance has residual uncertainty (recorded artifactually). Construct validity: emulator‑observed faults are a conservative proxy for operational harm but may not capture traffic‑dependent, temporal, or multi‑device interactions present in production. External validity: experiments used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic/emulated topologies; results do not generalize across all models, dialects, or production hardware. Conclusion validity: with zero baseline failures the planned power to detect a 0.20 absolute reduction could not be realized; the preregistered power assumption required a nonzero baseline error rate.

Reproducibility and artifact‑grounded diagnostics. All raw_results.jsonl, task_manifest.jsonl, execution/scoring traces, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json, execution/model_configuration.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl are archived and hashed in the evidence bundle. The bootstrap parameters (seed = 1729, resamples = 10000) and analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) are recorded. Reproduction steps are: (1) inspect execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl for declared model, adapter, and task payloads; (2) confirm provider_call_audit and deterministic_reconciliation.json for completed call counts; (3) apply paired_binary_analysis_v1 to execution/raw_results.jsonl to reproduce contingency counts and inference results. Representative artifact paths are provided in the evidence manifest.

Operational implications. The absence of baseline faults on this constrained corpus suggests that modern LLMs can be highly accurate for structured intent→config tasks when prompts, dialects, and task constraints are narrow. Responsible deployment, however, requires broader stress testing, adversarial tasks, multi‑model sampling, and human oversight; verifiers remain valuable when generator error prevalence or real‑world complexity increases.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics (72 confirmatory pairs) to measure whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator‑observed faults; consequently the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). The evidence‑grounded conclusion is conditional: verifier benefit depends on generator error prevalence and task realism. To measure verifier utility under realistic error regimes we recommend experimental contracts that permit independent/multiple stochastic generations per condition, adversarial/fault‑injection task sets, and multi‑model comparisons. We release deterministic execution manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support replication and targeted follow‑on studies.

References

[1] N. Tu, S. Nam, J. W.‑K. Hong, "Intent‑Based Network Configuration Using Large Language Models," Network and Emerging Markets (Nem), 2024.
[2] Z. Wang et al., "Intent‑Driven Network Management with Multi‑Agent LLMs: The Confucius Framework," Proc. ACM Symp., 2025.
[3] R. Cadenas, "Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments," SSRN, 2026.
[4] P. Kazemian, M. T. Chang, H. Zeng, G. Varghese, N. McKeown, S. Whyte, "Real time network policy checking using header space analysis," 2013.

Preregistration: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 was preregistered and frozen before observing outcomes (preregistration manifest SHA‑256: 8822fb18cb9c3e05aa405d8a1db7373ab6dc5a60ff928e4ae357da5fb73475b3). No human manual manuscript editing or content insertion occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is a residual uncertainty recorded in the archived configuration.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
